chunks: "The divider has to balance two things. If the resistance is too high, the feedback pin is no longer ideal.
The pin draws a little bias current, and that flows through the top resistor and shifts the output, so the error is I FB times R 1 .
Leakage on the board or flux residue across the bottom resistor does the same.
The node is also high impedance, so it picks up noise from the switch node, and the resistance forms a low-pass pole with the pin and stray capacitance.
That pole can land near the loop crossover and eat phase margin, so the converter can ring or oscillate. If the resistance is too low, the divider itself becomes a load. At 3.
3 volts, a 5. 5 kilohms divider draws 600 microamps all the time.
That barely matters at an amp of load, but at light load or on a battery it can be a big fraction of the current and ruins efficiency in PFM or sleep.
So I'd pick the divider in the tens to a few hundred kΩ range, 10 k to 100 k for R 2 is typical, check the datasheet's recommended maximum, and use 1% or better resistors, kept close to the FB pin."
